title: Sepsis with a surgical source
subtitle: Source control is the treatment

sources.title: International guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock
Guidelines for the management of intra-abdominal infections
Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network annual report

red_flags.text: Hypotension persisting after fluid, or a lactate above 4 mmol/L. This is septic shock, not sepsis.
New confusion or agitation in an elderly surgical patient. Often the only sign before collapse.
A source that cannot drain itself: an obstructed duct, an undrained collection, dead bowel, an infected implant.
Deterioration despite 24 to 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics. The source has not been controlled.
Mottled skin, prolonged capillary refill or a falling urine output with a normal blood pressure.

do_now.text: Cultures where they will not delay treatment, then broad-spectrum antimicrobials within the first hour for septic shock.
Fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloid, reassessing after each bolus rather than running a fixed volume.
Measure lactate and repeat it. A lactate that does not fall is a source that is not controlled.
Identify the anatomical source in the first hours and commit to how it will be controlled.

assess.text: Screen and score. Use the score to escalate care, never to withhold it from a patient who looks unwell.
Systematic hunt for the source: abdomen, wound and drains, chest, urinary tract, lines and implants, soft tissue, perineum.
Examine the perineum and the back of every diabetic patient. Fournier gangrene and a sacral abscess are missed by not looking.
Review every device: central line, urinary catheter, drain, mesh, prosthesis. An infected device is a source.
Recent antimicrobials, hospital exposure and prior resistant isolates change empiric choice more than the syndrome does.

investigate.text: Two sets of blood cultures, plus culture of the suspected site, before or alongside the first dose.
Lactate, gas, FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, coagulation, procalcitonin where it is used locally for de-escalation.
Contrast CT of the likely compartment is the highest-yield single investigation for an undrained surgical source.
Ultrasound at the bedside for the patient too unstable to travel: free fluid, hydronephrosis, a collection, cardiac filling.
Renal function drives dosing as much as the organism does.

resuscitate.text: Vasopressors for a mean arterial pressure target once fluid responsiveness is exhausted; start them through a peripheral line rather than delay for central access.
Choose the empiric regimen against the local antibiogram and ICMR data, not a memorised default; then de-escalate on culture.
Dose the first dose fully. Renal adjustment applies to subsequent doses, not the loading one.
Stress-dose steroid only for shock refractory to fluid and vasopressor.

definitive.text: Source control as early as the patient's physiology allows, and generally within 6 to 12 hours of recognition.
Choose the least invasive effective option: percutaneous drainage of a discrete collection beats a laparotomy in a physiologically fragile patient.
Remove or exchange an infected device. Antibiotics do not sterilise a colonised prosthesis.
Re-look and re-image if the patient fails to improve. Undrained sepsis is the commonest reason for a failed regimen.

escalate.text: Critical care review at the point of persisting hypotension or a rising lactate, not after the vasopressor is running.
Interventional radiology for a drainable collection; theatre for anything that will not drain through a tube.
Antimicrobial stewardship review at 48 to 72 hours, with a documented stop or step-down date.

notes: The surgical version of the sepsis bundle has one extra element and it is the one that matters: find and control the source.
Antibiotics buy hours. They do not treat pus, dead tissue, an obstructed duct, or an infected implant.
A patient who is not improving on the right antibiotic almost never needs a broader antibiotic.
